title: Why Carpet Buckles and Ripples (And When Re-Stretching Beats Replacing)
meta: Carpet buckles when it was never power-stretched, humidity swells the backing or the pad fails. Wills Flooring on when a Lynnwood re-stretch beats replacing.
keywords: why does carpet buckle, carpet ripples after cleaning, carpet re-stretching vs replacing, loose wrinkled carpet fix, carpet installation Lynnwood WA

blocks.lead: Carpet buckles and ripples for four main reasons: it was installed with a knee kicker instead of a power stretcher, humidity or a wet cleaning swelled the backing, heavy furniture was dragged across it, or the pad or backing has broken down with age. The first three can usually be fixed with a re-stretch. The last one means replacing.
blocks.detail: The test is simple: if the carpet is under about eight years old, the backing is still stiff and the ripples showed up after a specific event, re-stretch it. If it is older, the backing crackles when you fold a corner, or the ripples keep coming back, it is done. Replacing it is $0.99 per sq ft in labor at Wills Flooring, $30 per stair, plus the carpet and pad.

blocks.html: The call usually comes in after a steam cleaning or a humid August: the hallway carpet in an Alderwood split-level has a wave running across it, or the family room in a Martha Lake rambler ripples where the vacuum catches. A common Reddit thread asks whether that means the carpet is ruined. Usually it does not. Ripples are a symptom, and the cause decides whether a re-stretch fixes it for good or whether you are paying to prop up a carpet at the end of its life.

blocks.text: The real causes of buckling, in order of how often we see them

items.title: Never power-stretched
items.text: A knee kicker seats carpet on the tack strip; a power stretcher pulls it tight across the whole room. Crews in a hurry skip the stretcher, the carpet looks fine for a year, then it relaxes and waves appear down the longest run of the room.

items.title: Humidity and wet cleaning
items.text: The latex layer that binds most carpet backings expands when damp. A rental steam cleaner that over-wets the carpet, or a Lynnwood house with no air conditioning in a muggy August, lets it swell. Tight carpet recovers as it dries; loosely stretched carpet stays rippled.

items.title: Dragging heavy furniture
items.text: Sliding a sofa or a loaded dresser pushes a wave of carpet ahead of it and can pop it off the tack strip. The ripple sits near a wall, shaped like the path the furniture took.

items.title: Backing or pad failure
items.text: After 10 to 15 years the latex dries out and the secondary backing separates from the primary, called delamination. The carpet feels loose and lumpy and the pad may have crumbled. No stretch holds, because there is nothing solid left to stretch.

items.title: Loose tack strip or a bad seam
items.text: Tack strip that has pulled away from an old plywood subfloor, common in 1970s Lynnwood homes, releases the edge. An unsealed seam lets the two pieces creep apart and buckle along the seam line.

blocks.text: Re-stretch or replace? The honest test

a.title: Worth it when
items: The carpet is under about eight years old and the pile still looks good
The backing is stiff and does not crackle when you fold a corner
The ripples followed one event: a cleaning, a move, a humid month
There is enough carpet at the walls to trim after stretching

b.title: Time to replace when
items: It is 12 or more years old and worn in the walk paths anyway
You can feel the backing has gone soft or crunchy
Ripples came back within a year of the last stretch
The pad has crumbled or the subfloor is damp
Seams are frayed or the carpet has been patched more than once

blocks.text: How to diagnose it yourself in ten minutes

items.text: Find out when it was installed. Under eight years favors a stretch. Over twelve favors replacing regardless of the cause.
Pull the carpet off the tack strip in a closet and fold it back on itself. Stiff and springy means the backing is alive. Crackling latex or the two backings separating means it is done.

items.d: 3. Look at where the ripples are
items.text: Waves across the long axis of the room point to no power stretch. A ripple along one wall points to a dragged couch or loose tack strip. Ripples along a seam point to the seam.
A cleaning in the last month or a humid spell means the backing swelled. Give it two weeks with a dehumidifier. If it tightens back up, the carpet is fine but was stretched loosely.
Press hard with your heel in the walk path. If the pad feels crumbly or you can feel the subfloor through it, the pad is finished too.

blocks.text: Mistakes that make buckled carpet worse

items.html: Steam cleaning it again to "reset" it. More moisture swells the backing further. Dry it out first, then stretch.
Stretching with a knee kicker only. It is how the carpet got loose in the first place. A re-stretch needs a power stretcher across the full room.
Cutting out the ripple. Slicing a wave and gluing the edges makes a visible seam and does nothing about the slack. It always comes back.
Dragging furniture over it. Lift it or use sliders, especially in long, narrow Lynnwood townhome rooms where one drag pushes a wave the whole length.
Paying to stretch a 15-year-old carpet. The stretch may hold six months. New carpet is $0.99 per sq ft in labor plus material, so put the money there.

blocks.text: What to ask so your next carpet never buckles

items: Will the carpet be power-stretched in both directions, not just kicked in? Get it in writing.
What pad is going under it, and is it the density the mill specifies? Too soft a pad shortens the life of any carpet.
Will loose tack strip be replaced? In 1960s and 1970s Meadowdale and Alderwood homes it usually should be.
How are seams sealed? Seam sealer on every cut edge keeps seams from creeping apart.
Will the carpet acclimate in the house before it is installed?
What is the workmanship warranty? At Wills Flooring it is one year, and a carpet that ripples inside that year is our problem, not yours.

faq.q: Why did my carpet buckle after cleaning?
faq.a: Over-wetting swells the latex in the backing, and carpet that was not stretched tightly at install has nowhere to go but up. Dry the room thoroughly with fans or a dehumidifier for a week or two. If the ripples stay, the carpet needs a power stretch; if the carpet is old, it may need replacing.

faq.q: Can rippled carpet be fixed without replacing it?
faq.a: Usually, if the carpet is under about eight years old and the backing is still stiff. A carpet repair technician releases the carpet at one wall, power-stretches it across the room and trims the excess. Wills Flooring does not do re-stretching, but we will tell you honestly if that is the right fix.

faq.q: How do I know if the carpet backing has failed?
faq.a: Fold a corner back on itself in a closet. Healthy backing is stiff and springs back. Failed backing crackles, sheds a powdery latex, or lets the two backing layers separate. Once that happens the carpet cannot hold a stretch and replacement is the only real fix.

Not if it is installed correctly. That means a power stretcher across the full room in both directions, the pad density the manufacturer calls for, fresh tack strip where the old strip is loose, sealed seams and acclimating the carpet in the house before install. Ask for each of those in writing.

faq.q: Does humidity in Lynnwood cause carpet ripples?
faq.a: It contributes. Most Lynnwood homes have no air conditioning, and a muggy stretch in late summer can loosen a carpet that was stretched only with a knee kicker. Well-stretched carpet on a good pad tightens back up when the house dries out in fall.

faq.q: Should I replace the pad if I replace the carpet?
faq.a: Yes, almost always. Old pad has compressed in the walk paths and may have absorbed spills or pet accidents. New carpet on old pad flexes unevenly and works loose sooner. Labor is the published $0.99 per sq ft either way; the pad itself is quoted with the carpet at the free estimate.
